title: Azure Crosses $100B — Microsoft's AI Bet Is Paying Off
subtitle: Azure topped $100 billion in annual revenue, growth re-accelerated to 43%, and Copilot passed 30 million paid seats — then the stock posted its best single-day gain since 2008. The AI monetization debate is officially over.
summary: Microsoft's Q4 FY2026 was a blowout: revenue of $90B crushed estimates, Azure crossed $100B in annual revenue for the first time with growth re-accelerating to 43%, and Copilot hit 30M+ paid seats. After a brutal year of doubt, the stock surged on July 30 — and the numbers say the AI bet is finally paying off.

bodyHtml:
For months, the market treated Microsoft's AI story like a rumor that refused to become a receipt. The stock had fallen roughly 17% year to date, sat about 29% below its 52-week high, and traded at around 20x forward earnings — the kind of discount this franchise hasn't offered since long before the AI era began. Then the company reported fiscal Q4 earnings on July 29, and the crowd finally got its receipt. The next day, shares posted their best single-day gain since 2008.

The selloff wasn't random. The AI trade rotated violently through 2026 — every hyperscaler tripled down on data center spending, memory prices spiked, and investors started asking a fair question: who actually makes money from all this infrastructure? Microsoft, despite being the most obvious beneficiary, got swept up in the same de-rating. It was a textbook case of throwing the baby out with the bathwater.

The bull case was never complicated. Microsoft owns the enterprise distribution layer for AI — the default vendor for corporate software, the landlord of the cloud, and the partner of choice for the frontier labs. The bear case was equally simple: the spending was enormous, the monetization unproven, and Azure's growth had been decelerating for a year. Q4 2026 answered the bear case with a number the company had never hit before.

Azure crossed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time, up 41% year over year. Even better, the quarter itself accelerated to 43% growth, up from 40% in the prior quarter. Reacceleration is the rarest word in mega-cap tech right now. Most hyperscalers are fighting just to hold growth steady; Microsoft is bending the curve back up.

The headline numbers back it up. Total revenue hit $90 billion, up 18%, and blew past the $87.6 billion consensus. Adjusted EPS topped expectations by roughly 12%. Operating income rose to $40.6 billion, up 18%. Microsoft Cloud — the umbrella over Azure, Microsoft 365, and everything else — surpassed $214 billion for the fiscal year, up 27%, with $59.3 billion in the quarter alone. This is an enterprise the size of a small nation's economy, growing like a startup.

The AI monetization question — the one that kept the stock pinned at a discount all year — got its clearest answer yet. Microsoft 365 Copilot now has more than 30 million paid seats, and commercial remaining performance obligation jumped 84% year over year. That backlog number is the real story. Enterprises are pre-committing to years of Microsoft AI and cloud services faster than the company can build capacity for them.

The other worry was the checkbook, and management handled that too. Full-year fiscal 2026 capex hit another record, with $41 billion in the final quarter alone, and CFO Amy Hood left calendar 2026 spending guidance unchanged while committing to positive free cash flow through fiscal 2027. Compare that with rivals levering up to build. Microsoft is funding the biggest infrastructure buildout in its history off a balance sheet that still generates $70+ billion a year in free cash flow — and it still returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the quarter.

Even the side bets are paying. The quarter included a $3.2 billion gain from Microsoft's Anthropic investment, a reminder that the company's AI tentacles reach far beyond its own products. And the forward look is what really sent the stock into orbit: management guided Azure to 45% growth at constant currency for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Reacceleration, with guidance for more reacceleration, is about as close to a perfect earnings call as a mega-cap can have.

Now the honest part. At roughly 20x forward earnings, with growth accelerating and a commercial backlog up 84%, the market is still pricing Microsoft like a mature utility with an AI side project. The analyst consensus is a Strong Buy, and the mean price target implies roughly 15% upside from where shares settled after the pop. For a company executing this well, that's not demanding — that's cheap.

CEO Satya Nadella framed it perfectly: “We are advancing the frontier on the cost-to-outcome curve, ensuring every customer can turn tokens into business results.” That's the whole thesis in one sentence — Microsoft isn't selling compute, it's selling outcomes, and enterprises are buying at a record pace. The stock's year-long funk was a discount on doubt. The doubt is gone. The discount, for now, remains.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in MSFT. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
